activities.caption: rebuild the LLM pipeline, stage by stage
activities.name: tflPipelineOrder

config.prompt: Five stages, each operating on the output of the one before — rebuild the pipeline:
items: tokens: text chopped into sub-word units
embeddings: each token becomes a vector — language as geometry
attention: every token consults every other
pretraining: predict the next token, trillions of times
alignment: instruction tuning and RLHF shape the assistant
scaling laws: loss falls as a smooth power law
config.why: Each stage operates on the output of the one before — which is why a compromise made at tokenisation propagates all the way up.

activities.caption: pair the arithmetic with its meaning
activities.name: tflGeometryMatch

config.prompt: Language as geometry — pair each item with its consequence:

pairs.right: end up close together — interchangeable company

pairs.left: roughly 4 characters or ¾ of a word

config.why: None of this was programmed — it is the shadow that predicting-words-from-context casts onto geometry.

activities.anchor: the model reads text the way you do
activities.caption: find the faulty line — how the model reads
activities.name: tflTokensSpot

config.prompt: This summary contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: Neural networks eat numbers, so text is chopped into sub-word tokens.
Common words stay whole; rare ones split into pieces.
The model reads text the way you do — as words, or at least letters.
Counting the letters in a long word fails because the model sees chunks, not characters.
Tokenisation is a compromise of vocabulary size against sequence length.
config.correction: It reads tokens — and the mismatch explains a whole genre of famous failures: letter-counting, arithmetic slips on large numbers, wordplay that lands flat.
config.why: Tokenisation's seams show in behaviour whenever a task gets down to the character level — the input simply does not contain what the task asks about.

activities.anchor: The arithmetic cost is the quadratic term
activities.caption: which curve is attention's bill?
activities.name: tflQuadraticTrace

config.prompt: Attention compares every token with every other. Which curve shows attention compute as context length (x) grows?
config.why: Doubling the context quadruples that part of the compute — the reason long-context models are an engineering frontier, not a free lunch.

activities.caption: true or false — reading the attention weights
activities.name: tflAttentionJudge

statements.s: Attention is a routing computation — it decides which vectors get mixed into which.
statements.why: One part of the stack, alongside the per-position feed-forward network where much of the knowledge is stored.

statements.s: Attention highlights important words the way a highlighter does.
statements.why: It routes information between positions; interpreting individual weights as explanations has repeatedly failed.

statements.s: The same output can arise from different attention patterns.
statements.why: Which is exactly why model explanation is its own research field rather than a weights-reading exercise.

statements.s: Attention heads all learn the same function.
statements.why: Some learn to track syntax, some coreference, some position patterns — many heads in parallel.

activities.caption: drag the divider — completer to assistant
activities.name: tflAssistantCompare

config.prompt: The gap closed in post-training — drag between the two stages:

before.label: Raw predictor
before.text: Completes text: 'How do I make bread?' might continue '…the question many bakers ask' — fluent, worldly, and not listening.

after.label: Assistant
after.text: Instruction fine-tuning on curated question–answer pairs, then RLHF: humans rank outputs, a reward model learns the ranking — a small fraction of the compute, most of the difference.

config.why: The labels were free (self-supervision), but following instructions is a separate, deliberate stage — the difference between a document-finisher and something you can delegate to.

activities.caption: call the magnitude — the compute-optimal corpus
activities.name: tflChinchillaEstimate

config.prompt: Under Chinchilla's compute-optimal rule (roughly 20 training tokens per parameter), how many tokens does a 70-billion-parameter model want?
config.why: 70B × 20 ≈ 1.4 trillion tokens — models trained before this rule were undertrained, which is why Chinchilla's 70B beat its 280B sibling trained on 300B.
config.context: Loss falls as a smooth power law in model size, dataset size and compute — predictability that converted research into logistics.

activities.caption: design the successor — three architectures, three trade-offs
activities.name: tflSuccessorBranch

config.root: You are designing a post-transformer architecture. Every choice is a trade-off.

choices.label: Full attention — every pair of positions

recurrence.text: Training cannot parallelise across the sequence, and long-range information decays through the steps — the limitation attention was built to remove.

attention.text: Every pair of positions in one matrix multiplication — a GPU crunches thousands of tokens at once, the architecture the hardware wanted. The quadratic cost is the price.

sparse.text: Keep the scaling while shedding the n² term — sparse attention, linear attention, state-space models like Mamba. Whether any displaces vanilla attention at frontier scale is genuinely open.

config.why: The transformer is the architecture the hardware wanted — parallelism won over memory, and the research frontier is what comes after the quadratic bill.
